lesson.title: Comparatives: más, menos, mejor
lesson.subtitle: más... que, menos... que, tan... como, and irregular mejor/peor

hook.title: Why Spanish Never Adds '-er' to Adjectives
hook.content: In English, short adjectives add '-er' ('bigger, smaller, colder') while long adjectives use 'more' ('more important, more interesting'). Spanish uses one clean system for every regular adjective: place más ('more', with an accent!) or menos ('less') before the adjective, and close the comparison with que ('than'): más grande que ('bigger than'), menos importante que ('less important than')!

pattern.title: Equality (Tan... Como) and the Two Suppletives: Mejor & Peor
pattern.content:
• **Equality ('as [adj] as')**: tan + adjective + como (tan grande como 'as big as', tan importante como 'as important as').
• **Better & Worse**: Just as English says 'better' (never *gooder) and 'worse' (never *badder), Spanish says mejor ('better / best', cousin of English ameliorate!) and peor ('worse / worst', cousin of pejorative!) — never *más bueno or *más malo!
pattern.linguist_note: Latin magis ('more') won out in Iberian Romance (Spanish más, Portuguese mais), whereas plūs won out in Galloromance and Italic (French plus, Italian più).
pattern.trap_note: Notice the accent on más ('more'): with a tilde, más means 'more/most'; without a tilde, literary mas means 'but'!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: más, menos, mejor, peor, tan... como, más grande que
exercises.meaning: more / -er, less, better / best, worse / worst, as [adj] as, bigger than
exercises.explanation: más/menos... que handles inequality; tan... como handles equality; mejor/peor replace *más bueno/*más malo.

exercises.prompt: Spanish peor ('worse', from Latin peior) shares its root with which English adjective for a word or remark that disparages or makes something sound 'worse'?
exercises.meaning: a pejorative term is literally one that makes things look 'worse' (peor)!
exercises.explanation: Latin peior gave Spanish peor and English pejorative, while melior gave Spanish mejor and English ameliorate.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'This coffee is better than that one'?
options: Este café es mejor que ese
*Este café es más bueno que ese
exercises.target_answer: Este café es mejor que ese
exercises.meaning: This coffee is better than that one
exercises.explanation: mejor ('better') replaces *más bueno and links to the second item with que ('than').

exercises.target_answer: Madrid es más grande que Toledo
exercises.explanation: Madrid es + más grande + que + Toledo.

exercises.idea: say that this book is as important as that one (tan importante como ese)
cues: This book is → Este libro es
idea_parts: This book is → Este libro es
as important as → tan importante como
exercises.target_answer: Este libro es tan importante como ese
exercises.meaning: This book is as important as that one
exercises.explanation: Este libro es tan importante como ese — equality uses tan... como (without an accent on como!).

diagnosis.slip: used que instead of como after tan
diagnosis.cue: Inequality (más/menos) closes with que ('than'); equality (tan) closes with como ('as').

summary.outcome: Compare adjectives with más/menos... que, tan... como, and irregular mejor and peor.

use_example.german: Madrid es más grande que Toledo y este café es mejor que ese.
use_example.english: Madrid is bigger than Toledo and this coffee is better than that one.

summary.takeaway: más/menos/mejor/peor close with que ('than'); tan closes with como ('as').
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([2101] Superiority and Inferiority): build comparatives and superlatives ('the biggest' = el más grande).

más.english_meaning: more, most (with accent; mas without accent = 'but')
más.context_phrase: Madrid es más grande que Toledo.
más.etymology_derivation: más... que = 'more... than'; el/la más... = 'the most / -est'.

menos.context_phrase: Es menos caro que el hotel.
menos.context_translation: It is less expensive than the hotel.

mejor.context_phrase: Este vino es mejor que ese.
mejor.context_translation: This wine is better than that one.

tan.context_translation: It is as important as that.

como.etymology_derivation: Unaccented como closes equality comparisons: tan... como.

grande.etymology_derivation: Latin grandis. Invariable for gender: el hotel grande, la casa grande.

importante.etymology_derivation: Adjectives ending in -e do not change for gender: el punto importante, la idea importante.

bueno.etymology_derivation: Latin bonus gives English 'bonus' and Spanish bueno (o diphthongizes to ue under stress).

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
